Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law · Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

independent adjective

not under another’s rule or control

also independence, self-governing, sovereign, one’s own master, become independent, gain independence

classical

Cic. Verr. 2.1.18 (Lewis & Short, s.v. jūs)
M-O s.v. independent

suī jūris

phrase: the genitive of jūs, “of one’s own right”, usually with esse

independent, one’s own master

In law, a person in no one else’s power, neither a father’s nor a master’s; Cicero uses it of jurors too independent to be managed. Morgan–Owens gives it for an independent state, and suī jūris fierī for gaining independence (after Egger).

Other words

  • līber, lībera, līberum — free: of a state, independent

    declension · also used · classical · Caes. BG 1.45.3: līberam dēbēre esse Galliam; M-O s.v. independent

    The plain word for a free people (see free). Independence itself is lībertās (M-O s.v. independence).

  • suīs lēgibus ūtī — be self-governing: live under one’s own laws

    phrase: ūtor with the ablative · also used · classical · Caes. BG 1.45.3; M-O s.v. independence: facultās suīs lēgibus ūtendī (Egger)

    What Rome left to a free city or people it did not rule directly.

Examples

  • līberam dēbēre esse Galliam, quam bellō victam suīs lēgibus ūtī voluisset

    Gaul ought to be free, since the senate, though it had beaten her in war, had chosen to let her live under her own lawsCaes. BG 1.45.3

  • quod eōs in jūdicandō nimium suī jūris sententiaeque cognōsset

    because he knew them to be too independent, too much of their own mind, when they sat in judgmentCic. Verr. 2.1.18

See also freedom, free, state.
